author.author_institution: Department of Family Medicine, Michigan State University

list.listitem: Abortion is safer the earlier it is performed. B
If you are unable to provide accurate, empathetic pregnancy options counseling, refer to someone who can provide these services. C

Medication abortion is a safe, effective option for women with pregnancies of up to 70 days' gestation, especially for those in whom a surgical procedure would be difficult, such as women with extreme anxiety, morbid obesity, or gynecologic anomalies. A The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG, 2020) recommends use of combined mifepristone-misoprostol regimens as most effective. A

Reliable contraception should begin as soon as possible after an abortion. ACOG 2020 notes that almost all contraceptive methods, except IUDs and permanent contraception, can be safely initiated immediately on day 1 (mifepristone intake) of medication abortion. B

Although abortion is quite safe, the leading causes of death include anesthetic complications, infection, and hemorrhage. Maintain a high suspicion of endometritis even with mild symptoms after an abortion. B

background.definition: Induced abortion is a voluntary interruption of pregnancy that may be performed as an elective or medically-therapeutic procedure. Induced abortions use medication or surgical means to remove the products of conception from the uterus before the embryo or fetus is capable of independent life.

list.listitem: Of 6.4 million pregnancies in the United States annually, just under half are unintended. Rates of unintended pregnancy have decreased from 51% in 2008 to 45% in 2011. Of unintended pregnancies in 2011, 42% ended in abortion.

A total of 629,898 abortions were reported to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for 2019. Among 48 reporting areas with annual data since 2010, the abortion rate was 11.4 per 1,000 women aged 15 to 44 years and the abortion ratio 195 abortions per 1,000 live births. From 2010 to 2019, the total number, rate, and ratio of reported abortions decreased 18%, 21%, and 13%, respectively. Women in their 20s accounted for 56.9% of abortions. Nearly all (92.7%) abortions were performed at ≤13 weeks' gestation. In 2019, 42.3% of all abortions were medication abortions, an increase of 123% from 2010.
In a 2014 abortion patient survey, 65% of patients traveled less than 25 miles one-way to obtain services, 17% traveled 25 to 49 miles, and 18% traveled more than 50 miles.

Based on cross-sectional vital statistics information, following implementation of a restrictive abortion law in Texas, there was an increase in number of abortions performed at 12 weeks or later from 10.5% before the law to 14.5% after. In addition, women living 50 or more miles from the nearest facility had higher odds of second-trimester abortion than women living less than 10 miles from a facility (OR 1.2; 95% CI, 1.1-1.4).

In a scoping review of the impact of abortion-related care and abortion policies on economic outcomes internationally at the macroeconomic (large scale/general societal level), findings include the following:

On average, the cost of meeting a woman’s unmet need for modern contraceptive supplies and services for one year would amount to 3% to 12% of the average cost of treating a patient who requires post-abortion care.
Restrictive abortion laws impose financial hardships on abortion seekers, often resulting in costly delays (89% of American counties have no abortion providers within their county borders).
Studies have linked abortion legalization to women’s advancement in education and in the labor market.

Based on 2019 data from 30 areas that reported race by ethnicity data, non-Hispanic White women and non-Hispanic Black women accounted for the largest percentages of all abortions (33.4% and 38.4%, respectively), and Hispanic women and non-Hispanic women in the other race category accounted for smaller percentages (21.0% and 7.2%, respectively).
In 2019, most women (58.2%) had no previous abortions, 23.8% had one previous abortion, 10.5% previously had two abortions, and 7.5% previously had three or more abortions.

Denial of abortion due to presentation at up to three weeks over the facility gestational age limit with subsequent birth of a child appears to result in increased rates of poverty at 6 months and 4 years compared to women presenting near the facility gestational age limit who were granted abortion.
Previous abortion is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight (OR following one abortion 1.35 [95% CI, 1.20-1.52]) but not the birth of small for gestational age infants.

Authors of a meta-analysis found similar figures for women with a prior uterine evacuation for elective or spontaneous abortion, with increased risk of preterm birth (5.7% vs. 5.0%; OR 1.44; 95% CI, 1.09-1.90), low birthweight (7.3% vs. 5.9%; OR 1.41; 95% CI, 1.22-1.62), and small-for-gestational age infant (10.2% vs. 9.0%; OR, 1.19, 95% CI, 1.01-1.42) compared with controls.
Among teenage women, a history of abortion was associated with repeat teenage pregnancy risk (pooled OR 1.66; 95% CI, 1.08-2.54).
With the decline in abortion providers, 87% of counties have no abortion provider and 25% of women seeking an abortion travel 50 miles or more for their procedure.

The most common cited reasons for terminating an unwanted pregnancy are: Concern for or responsibility to other individuals (74%). Cannot afford a baby right now (73%). Having a baby would interfere with school/employment/ability to care for dependants (69%). Would be a single parent/relationship difficulties (48%). Has completed desired childbearing (38%).

Provision of free long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) at a family planning clinic was associated with a marked decrease in abortion rates based on a register-based cohort study in Finland. Rates were 80% lower than in the non-LARC cohort (16 abortions vs. 243; risk ratio 0.20, 95% CI, 0.11-0.32) and 74% lower than among matched control participants; RR 0.26, 95% CI, 0.15-0.43.

Before medication abortion is performed, ACOG 2020 recommends confirmation of pregnancy and estimating gestational age. For patients with regular menstrual cycles, a certain last menstrual period within the prior 56 days, and no signs, symptoms, or risk factors for ectopic pregnancy is sufficient (ie, a clinical examination or ultrasound is not necessary). B

A history of an unstable medical or psychiatric condition (eg, uncontrolled hypertension, seizure disorder, severe anxiety) should prompt consideration about the safety of performing an abortion as an outpatient procedure. C
Severe anemia or bleeding disorder with a history of uterine hemorrhage could lead to an unsafe amount of blood loss for an outpatient procedure. C
If a woman is unsure of her desire to give birth to a child, be prepared to discuss the options of parenting, adoption, and abortion. Refer if you are unable to discuss pregnancy options.

If termination is requested, elicit contraindications to outpatient elective termination (or refer to nearest abortion provider). If you believe an outpatient procedure would not be safe for this patient, expedite the appropriate referral by discussing the case with an abortion provider.

ACOG 2020 recommends confirmation of pregnancy and estimating gestational age. For patients with regular menstrual cycles, a certain last menstrual period within the prior 56 days, and no signs, symptoms, or risk factors for ectopic pregnancy is sufficient (ie, a clinical examination or ultrasound is not necessary).

Physical conditions that may prohibit an outpatient procedure include very severe anemia, history of bleeding disorder, uncontrolled hypertension, uncontrolled seizure disorder, or history of myocardial infarction. Morbid obesity can inhibit visualization and interfere with the ability to perform an outpatient procedure.

Women with severe anxiety leading to an inability to cooperate with the surgical procedure can sometimes benefit from oral or intravenous anxiolytics; other women may need general anesthesia to proceed safely.

Treat current reproductive system infection prior to abortion. Severe fibroids or anatomical variation may require ultrasound guidance for surgical abortion. When gestational age is early enough, these women are excellent candidates for medication abortion.
Discuss drug allergies and past anesthesia complications.

Necessary tests will usually be performed by the abortion provider. If the clinician will not be performing the abortion procedure, perform only those tests necessary to provide accurate referral. Consider the following tests: Urine pregnancy test. Hematocrit: if severe anemia, may not be appropriate for outpatient procedure. The National Abortion Federation guidelines do not recommend Rh testing and anti-D immunoglobulin for women presenting for early abortion. This is supported by a study of 644 women undergoing medication or procedural abortion at less than 12 weeks gestation. If the patient complains of vaginitis or symptoms of pelvic inflammatory disease, evaluate and treat as indicated.

If there are clinical indications for an ultrasound examination before medication abortion, ACOG 2020 recommends transabdominal ultrasonography, reserving transvaginal ultrasonography for situations in which further clarification is required.

The clinician's role is to provide appropriate counseling and referral to an abortion provider, if needed. Patients who choose abortion should be counseled about all methods available as well as the risks, advantages, disadvantages, and the different features of these options. If the clinician feels unable to discuss pregnancy options or provide counseling, the woman must be referred to someone who can provide these services.
The earlier in pregnancy an abortion is performed, the lower the risk of complications. If a woman has the desire to discuss termination with an abortion provider, prompt referral should be made.

Counsel patients that medication abortion failure rates, especially continuing pregnancy rates, increase as gestational age approaches 10 weeks. In addition, ACOG 2020 recommends that patients be counseled regarding the teratogenicity of misoprostol (congenital anomalies such as limb defects with or without facial paralysis, when used during the first trimester) in the event of an unsuccessful medication abortion.

Medication abortion is an acceptable option to surgical abortion in selected, carefully counseled, and informed women. A ACOG 2020 considers most patients at 70 days of gestation or less who desire abortion eligible for medication abortion.

Medication abortion with mifepristone 200 mg orally followed by misoprostol 800 mcg buccally or vaginally 24 to 48 hours later carries less risk of gastrointestinal side effects and received FDA approval in 2016. A
Modern surgical abortion at less than 13 weeks of gestation is performed with vacuum aspiration, which has fewer complications than previously used dilation and curettage. A
Abortion after 13 weeks of gestation is safest when done by dilation and extraction, often after cervical preparation with prostaglandin or osmotic dilators. A

Contraception should be discussed and supplies provided for women undergoing an abortion. Contraception should begin as soon as possible. C ACOG 2020 notes that almost all contraceptive methods, except IUDs and permanent contraception, can be safely initiated immediately on day 1 (mifepristone intake) of medication abortion. B

Medication abortion is an option for women with pregnancies at 70 days or less. Ideally, women should have access to emergency services in the event of complications such as hemorrhage or infection. The gestational age limits may change if additional studies demonstrate safety and efficacy.

AOCG 2020 recommends patient counseling before medication abortion to include when patients should contact their clinician in the case of heavy bleeding (soaking more than two maxi pads per hour for 2 consecutive hours) and when to access urgent intervention.

Based on a nation-wide cohort study of 86,437 early medication abortions, the proportion of surgical interventions increased from 3.5% in the 5th to 6th gestational week to 10.3% in week 9 (OR 3.2; 95% CI, 2.9-3.6).

A prospective cohort study of 264 pregnant individuals between 9 and 22 weeks found that 75% of patients were able to self-medicate a completed abortion without additional health care services. Only 5% underwent a vacuum aspiration or dilatation and curettage to complete the abortion, and less than 2% received a transfusion. Less than 10% did not have a completed abortion or were unsure whether the abortion was completed.

First trimester medication abortion at 9 weeks or less is highly effective and similar to early surgical abortion with no differences in major adverse events between groups, based on a nation-wide cohort study of 86,437 early medication abortions. Women undergoing medication abortion were more likely to undergo unanticipated aspiration for ongoing pregnancy or persistent pain, or bleeding than women undergoing surgical abortion (2.1% vs. 0.6%, respectively).
ACOG (2020) recommends combined mifepristone-misoprostol regimens as most effective.

The current FDA-approved regimen is 200 mg mifepristone followed by 800 mcg misoprostol buccally; this second dose, taken at 24-48 hours after the oral dose, can be administered intravaginally. This regimen has half the rates of nausea and vomiting.

In December 2021, the FDA revised their restrictions regarding mifepristone access under the risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program. While previously requiring the drug be "dispensed to patients only in certain health-care settings, specifically clinics, medical offices, and hospitals, by or under the supervision of a certified prescriber", they now state that mifepristone can be prescribed by or under the supervision of a certified healthcare provider, that patients must sign a Prescriber Agreement Form after counseling and prior to prescribing the drug, and the drug should be dispensed through a certified pharmacy. As of this writing, this statement does not appear on the FDA REMS website.

In a meta-analysis of 20 trials of medication abortion, outpatient regimens with mifepristone followed in 24-48 hours by buccal misoprostol were found to be highly effective for pregnancy termination through 63 days of gestation (96.7%; 95% CI, 96.5%-96.8%). Authors of a Cochrane review of first trimester medical abortion confirmed these findings. Buccal and sublingual misoprostol have similar efficacy to vaginal administration but more side effects.

ACOG 2020 notes that patients can safely and effectively use both mifepristone and misoprostol at home for medication abortion. Authors of a Cochrane review confirmed that self-administering early medical abortion was as effective as provider-administered procedures for abortion success; for the two included RCTs, the RR was 0.99, 95% CI, 0.97-1.01 (919 participants; moderate certainty of evidence). The authors were uncertain if there are any differences in complications requiring surgical intervention.

In a second meta-analysis of 19 studies (3 RCTs and 16 non-randomized studies) with 11,576 women seeking abortion up to 9 weeks gestation, authors also found no differences in abortion success comparing home-based and clinic-based administration of medication abortion.

Of note, 6 women (approximately 1 in 100,000) died of sepsis from Clostridium sordellii after medication abortion using intravaginal misoprostol. It is unclear why these infections occurred. Anecdotally, in Europe, where buccal dosing is preferred, there have been no cases of this infection. Subsequently, Planned Parenthood Federation of America changed from vaginal to oral or buccal misoprostol. No further cases of sepsis were reported.

listitem.strong: Comparative studies of dose, regimen and timing of medication abortion

list.listitem: Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 trials found no difference between administration intervals for misoprostol following mifepristone of 8-72 hours (lower success rates were reported with intervals less than 8 hours).

However, authors of a meta-analyses of three RCTs with 1280 patients showed no differences in ongoing pregnancy, hemorrhage requiring transfusion, or incomplete abortion with need for surgical intervention between simultaneous and interval administration of mifepristone and misoprostol for abortion up to 10 weeks’ gestation.

A large RCT sponsored by the World Health Organization demonstrated equivalency for 100 or 200 mg of mifepristone followed by 800 mcg misoprostol intravaginally (92%-93.5% complete abortion vs. 91.7%-93.2%).

Misoprostol alone can also be effective for early pregnancy termination; in one RCT of medication versus surgical abortion, 800 mcg of misoprostol resulted in complete abortion in 94% of women (vs. 96% in the surgical group) with fewer women reporting pain and use of analgesics. Two women in the misoprostol group had diarrhea requiring medication.

Authors of a 2011 Cochrane review found that misoprostol alone is less effective than combined regimen of mifepristone/prostaglandin (RR 3.76 95% CI, 2.30-6.15). ACOG 2020 recommends use of a misoprostol-only regimen if a combined mifepristone-misoprostol regimen is not available.

Authors of a more recent systematic review of misoprostol alone found 38 papers reporting on 53 trial groups including 12,829 women but using different methods such as different routes, amount per dose and number of doses. Overall, 22.0% (95% CI, 18.8%-25.5%) had surgical uterine evacuation and, of the 6,359 evaluable women, 6.8% (95% CI, 5.3%-8.5%) had ongoing pregnancies. The most effective misoprostol-only regimens involved an 800 mcg dose, 3 or more doses, non-oral route of administration, moistening tablets prior to vaginal insertion if that route is chosen, and a delay of 3 to 7 days before considering surgical evacuation. With respect to safety, 26 of 12,184 evaluable women (0.7%, 95% CI, 0.4%-1.0%) were transfused or hospitalized for abortion-related reasons.

A retrospective cohort study suggests that the same-day start of medication abortion for patients with LMP within 42 days and an initial ultrasound result showing no gestational sac is a reasonable option, for both efficacy and safety. Women with major risk factors for (or symptoms suggesting) ectopic pregnancy were not eligible for same-day medication abortion in this study. A larger randomized controlled trial is necessary to verify the relative efficacy and safety of same-day initiation of medication abortion versus delay-for-diagnosis of intrauterine pregnancy before medication abortion.

A study identified 1504 women with an empty sac or sac-like structure without an embryonic pole or yolk sac on vaginal ultrasound and randomized them to either early medication abortion immediately after enrollment, or standard medication abortion after confirmation of the pregnancy. Early medication abortion was as effective as delaying treatment until intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed with respect to complete abortion. The reason for failed abortion differed between the groups, with ongoing pregnancy more likely in the early group and surgical intervention needed more often in the standard care group.

Bleeding, cramping, and passage of the pregnancy usually happen within 4 hours of taking misoprostol. Duration of pain for most patients is no longer than 24 hours after misoprostol administration and the most severe pain occurs approximately 2.5 to 4 hours after misoprostol use and lasts about 1 hour. Bleeding can range from similar to a heavy period to very heavy bleeding with blood clots the size of grapefruit. Cramping is usually well tolerated; ibuprofen (400-600 mg every 6-8 hours) may be sufficient for pain relief, but a narcotic is usually prescribed and 50% of women will use it.
ACOG 2020 recommends nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain management in patients undergoing medication abortion.

A meta-analysis of pain control found that prophylactic analgesics (acetaminophen, acetaminophen with codeine, ibuprofen or alverine) did not reduce medical abortion pain; use of ibuprofen after onset of cramping was helpful in reducing pain and subsequent analgesic use.

Lack of benefit of prophylactic pain medication was confirmed in a recent RCT of 563 patients in which neither tramadol or ibuprofen/metoclopramide co-administered with misoprostol and repeated 4 hours later resulted in a clinically meaningful lowering of mean maximum pain scores or overall abortion satisfaction.

listitem.strong: Medication abortion in more advanced pregnancy

list.listitem: Authors of a Cochrane review of second trimester medication termination concluded that the combination of mifepristone and vaginal misoprostol (preferably given at 3-hourly intervals) appeared to have the highest efficacy and shortest abortion time interval. Another metaanalysis found somewhat greater efficacy in vaginal versus sublingual misoprostol, although women preferred the latter.

In an RCT of 130 women at 13-24 weeks of gestation, 400 mcg of either vaginal or buccal misoprostol given every 3 hours for up to six doses had similar success rates for complete abortion (78% vs. 83%, respectively) and similar side effects but vaginal administration was associated with a shorter induction-to-abortion interval (25 ± 17 hours vs. 40 ± 29 hours, respectively).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 38 small RCTs found use of vaginal misoprostol for second and third trimester termination of pregnancy to be comparable to other prostaglandin preparations (eg, cervagem, prostaglandin E2 and prostaglandin F2alpha), and more effective than oral misoprostol administration. However, information on maternal safety was limited.
ACOG 2020 concluded that medication abortion can be provided safely and effectively by telemedicine with a high level of patient satisfaction.

Telemedicine-delivered medication abortion services were as safe as in-person services based on a retrospective cohort of 8765 telemedicine and 10,405 women from 13 Planned Parenthood health centers. Back-up services are needed for women who experience adverse events which occurred in 0.18% of the telemedicine group and 0.32% of the in-person treatment group.

In a retrospective cohort study in 3 US clinics (1727 abortions without screening tests and 649 with screening ultrasound and pelvic exam), the outcomes for medication abortion at less than 77 days' gestation with and without ultrasound screening and pelvic examination were comparable in this observational study. Limitations of the study were high loss to follow-up (38%), especially in the no-test group, and a more rural population in the no-test group.

A UK before and after study looked at the implementation of telehealth no test (including no ultrasound) medical abortion services for gestations less than 10 weeks. They concluded that it was safe and that the time to receipt of medicine was shortened by 4 days.

Authors of a systematic review of telemedicine for provision of abortion services reported high rates of success, safety and satisfaction. Outcome reports were as follows: 0% to 1.9% for continuing pregnancy, 93.8% to 96.4% for complete abortion, 0.9 to 19.3% for surgical evacuation, 0% to 0.7% for blood transfusion, 0.07% to 2.8% for hospitalization, and 64% to 100% for satisfaction.

In a case series of 615 Polish women who underwent medication abortion via telemedicine, women who had abortions at >9 weeks of gestation had higher rates of visits to the hospital within 1 day for complaints related to the abortion compared to women who were <9 weeks of gestation (11.7% vs. 3.3%, respectively; adjusted OR 3.82, 95% CI, 1.90-7.69).
ACOG (2020) does not recommend routine use of prophylactic antibiotics.

Based on observational data, the addition of antibiotic prophylaxis may increase safety. Authors determined that for every 1150 women treated with 200 mg oral mifepristone followed 24 to 48 hours later by 800 mcg buccal misoprostol and doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, one serious infection is avoided.

ACOG 2020 notes that almost all contraceptive methods, except IUDs and permanent contraception, can be safely initiated immediately on day 1 (mifepristone intake) of medication abortion and all contraceptive methods can be initiated after successful medication abortion.

Insertion of etonogestrel implants at the same time as administration of mifepristone compared to implanting after the abortion did not influence failure rates (3.9% and 3.8% required surgery to complete the abortion, respectively) or 6-month pregnancy rates (0.5% and 1.5%, respectively), although patient satisfaction was higher in the former group.

In one RCT, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate administered with mifepristone increased the risk of ongoing pregnancy compared to administration after completion of the abortion (8/220 [3.6%] vs. 2/226 [0.9%]); there were similar rates of need for surgery to complete the abortion (6.4% and 5.3%, respectively) and repeat pregnancy at 6 months (2.3% and 3.2%, respectively).

Immediate administration of oral contraceptives (OCs) following medication or surgical abortions appears to reduce vaginal bleeding time and amount, shorten the menstruation recovery period, increase endometrial thickness 2 to 3 weeks after abortion. Among women randomized to OCs in combination with traditional Chinese medicine compared to control women, there was a reduce the risk of incomplete abortion (RR 0.06) and unintended pregnancies (RR 0.06).

Vacuum aspiration or suction curettage is the most commonly used abortion procedure in the United States. It is an outpatient procedure performed within 14 weeks of gestation through dilation of the cervix (through graduated instrumentation or osmotic dilators) followed by suction evacuation.

Complication rates in a Canadian population-based retrospective study were lower for high volume vs. low volume (<10th percentile of yearly volume) providers with an adjusted OR for severe adverse events of 1.6 per 1000 procedures; 95% CI, 1.5-1.7) vs. 3.7 per 1000 procedures; 95% CI, 3.2-4.2).

Surgical abortion can be performed with a manual vacuum aspirator (MVA) within 12 weeks of gestation. This MVA is quiet, portable, and the products of conception are often easy to identify. Studies do not show that any one procedure (MVA, electrical VA, dilation and curettage [D&C]) is superior but MVA may be more difficult after 9 weeks gestation and duration of procedure is shorter with VA than D&C. Pain, patient satisfaction, and long-term fertility have not been evaluated.
In an RCT, oxytocin administration following first-trimester surgical abortion conferred no benefit on postoperative bleeding.

strong.em: Analgesia and anesthesia for first trimester abortion

list.listitem: Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or benzodiazepines are commonly provided 30-60 minutes prior to the procedure. In one RCT, providing 10 mg oral midazolam vs. placebo in addition to ibuprofen and a paracervical block slightly reduced preprocedural anxiety, but did not reduce pain or anxiety associated with uterine aspiration during first-trimester surgical abortions.

Local anesthesia by paracervical block (PCB) is usually used. Some providers offer intravenous or general anesthesia, though general anesthesia results in more than twice the rate of serious complications.

Transcutaneous nerve stimulation using high frequency and high intensity, was non-inferior to IV sedation (fentanyl, midazolam) for aspiration pain during first trimester abortion in an RCT with 109 patients.
In one study, self-administration of lidocaine gel before first-trimester surgical abortion was noninferior to PCB for pain.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that no local anesthetic technique, including PCB, provided reliable pain control in the 17 studies included. With respect to pain control for first trimester surgical abortion, another Cochrane review found decreased pain following conscious sedation, general anesthesia, and listening to music. Use of a 10% lidocaine spray with PCB may be useful.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found use of nitrous oxide in addition to local anesthesia and/or minimal sedation reduced perioperative pain during first trimester abortion. There was no effect on post-operative pain or nausea/vomiting.
Preoperative adjunctive gabapentin with paracervical block did not reduce pain during uterine aspiration based on an RCT of 111 women.

Second trimester abortion can be performed through induction of labor with prostaglandins and intraamniotic instillations alone or combined with Pitocin. These procedures comprise 1% of abortions and become more expensive if they take several days in a hospital setting.

Surgical second-trimester procedures include D&C, rarely used because of potential complications, and D&E, also called dilatation and extraction (D&X). D&E is the procedure referred to as partial-birth abortion. The cervix is dilated to 1.5-2.0 cm using laminaria or other means, the fetus is removed with forceps, and then suction is used to complete evacuation of the uterus. The D&E procedure is considered safer, faster, and less expensive than methods requiring medical induction of labor.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 2 trials found surgical D&E to be more effective for second trimester abortion than either intra-amniotic instillation of prostaglandin F2 alpha or induction with mifepristone and misoprostol; women randomized to D&E had fewer adverse events (OR 0.06; 95% CI, 0.01-0.76), fewer hospital stays, less pain, and comparable patient acceptability compared to those randomized to mifepristone/misoprostol.

In an RCT of prophylactic administration of 30 units of oxytocin in 500 mL of IV fluid or 500 mL of IV fluid alone initiated on speculum placement for 160 women undergoing D&E, there was no significant difference in the primary outcome of bleeding interventions (eg, uterine massage, uterotonics) between groups (7.3% vs. 16.7%; 9.4% difference, 95% CI -21% to 1.9%). There was a significant benefit of oxytocin on hemorrhage of 500 ml or more (3.7% vs. 21.8%) or 1000 ml or more (1.2% vs. 10.3%) but no differences in non-bleeding complications.
Prophylactic intramuscular (IM) methylergonovine maleate given after D&E at 20 to 24 weeks resulted in more episodes of excessive bleeding in an RCT of 284 patients.

Osmotic dilators or pharmacologic agents (mifepristone 200 mg, misoprostol, 400 µg either vaginally or sublingually) prior to first trimester abortion appear to reduce procedure time but is associated with some side effects. Nitrous oxide donors are inferior to prostaglandins for first-trimester cervical ripening and associated with more side effects.

Authors of a systematic review of 18 RCTs with 8538 patients for the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) found that cervical priming with misoprostol decreased the force needed to dilate the cervix for first trimester surgical abortion and reduced the risk of incomplete abortion, but increased preoperative bleeding compared to no priming. Preoperative bleeding, however, was reduced when sublingual misoprostol was given 1 hour before abortion compared with 3 hours before. The authors recommend use of routine cervical priming before first trimester surgical abortion with 400 µg misoprostol or, if misoprostol cannot be used, 200 mg oral mifepristone.

Interestingly, in an RCT of 110 women undergoing first trimester abortion under paracervical block, cervical priming with 200 mg of oral mifepristone 36 hours before surgery reduced perioperative pain compared to 400 µg buccal misoprostol given 3 hours before surgery.

With respect to surgical abortion at 14 to 24 weeks gestation, based on 15 RCTs with 2454 patients, authors concluded that osmotic dilators, misoprostol, or mifepristone should be used before abortion for pregnancies at 14+0 to 16+0weeks' gestation; osmotic dilators or misoprostol for pregnancies at 16+1 to 19+0 weeks' gestation; and osmotic dilators alone or with mifepristone for pregnancies at 19+1 to 24+0 weeks' gestation. Limited data from 3 papers did not show differences in procedure time or need for manual dilation between adjunctive misoprostol with osmotic dilators after 16 weeks.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that osmotic dilators provided superior cervical dilation when compared to prostaglandins alone or when combined with prostaglandins, but this difference did not appear to result in differences in procedure time or complication rates..

In an RCT comparing osmotic dilators alone, dilators plus 400 micrograms buccal misoprostol 3 hours preoperatively, and dilators plus 200 mg oral mifepristone during dilator placement for D&E, there was no difference in operative time, the primary outcome, between groups. With respect to secondary outcomes, adjunctive medication appeared to facilitate dilation and mifepristone was better tolerated than misoprostol.

Paracervical block can be used to reduce the pain of laminaria insertion with a median pain score of 13 mm vs. 54 mm among patients receiving sham blocks in one small trial. In this study, patient satisfaction with laminaria insertion was increased following paracervical block.

In an RCT of 39 women, IV sedation performed better for pain relief than nitrous oxide, with 7 women in the nitrous group (36.8%) requiring conversion to IV sedation. No women in the IV sedation group required additional pain medication.

In a cohort study of 2,523 (56%) second-trimester abortions completed under deep sedation without tracheal intubation, there were 2 cases of pulmonary aspiration (0.08%, 95% CI, 0.01%-0.29%), 4 cases of upper airway obstruction (0.016%, 95% CI, 0.04%-0.41%), and one case of lingual nerve injury (0.04%, 95% CI, 0.001%-0.22%).

Partial-birth abortion, a non-medical term, refers to intact dilation and extraction. A ban on this procedure was signed into law in 2003 and the decision was upheld in the U.S. Supreme Court in 2007. With the current partial-birth abortion ban, providers must ensure that the fetus is not alive before it is removed. The American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) statement on the US Supreme Court decision to uphold the Partial Birth Abortion Ban of 2003 discusses the impact of this legislation.
As of March 2016, 32 states have enacted bans. Additional information can be accessed through the Allan Guttmacher Institute.

An intrauterine device can be safely inserted directly after surgical abortion; six-month expulsion rates appear be slightly higher (5% vs. 2.7%), but IUD use at 6 months is higher with immediate insertion.
Dronabinol, a cannabinoid, did not reduce the maximum level of pain experienced following medication abortion in an RCT of 77 women.
Auricular acupressure or acupuncture was not more effective than placebo in reducing pain or anxiety scores in an RCT of 177 patients undergoing first trimester vacuum aspiration.
Abortion has not been linked to depression; however, referral to a mental health provider may be useful for women with a history of mood disorder or victims of rape or sexual abuse.

If the abortion is sought because of a serious maternal health indication, feelings of loss may be more prominent. Exhale is a toll-free after-abortion talkline: 1-866-4 EXHALE (1-866-439-4253) or www.4exhale.org.
For all postprocedure complications, first advise the patient to consult with their abortion provider.
Hemorrhage: If severe, refer to nearest emergency department.

Infection: Signs of endometritis should be evaluated. Signs of Clostridium sordellii infection may be subtle (eg, abdominal pain, bloating, and nausea, with or without fever). Despite signs of mild illness, white blood count will be elevated. Broad-spectrum antibiotics and inpatient monitoring are required.

Medication abortion: Complication rates from a study of 43,153 women treated at Planned Parenthood affiliates in 2003 are: ongoing pregnancy, 0.33%; hemorrhage requiring emergency department treatment, 0.11%; infection requiring hospitalization, 0.016%; and undiagnosed ectopic pregnancy, 0.005%. Complication rates from a Finnish national registry of second trimester compared with first trimester medical abortions were increased risk of surgical evacuation (about one third of the women following second trimester abortion; OR 15.2; 95% CI, 12.8-18.0) and infection (OR 2.1; 95% CI, 1.5-2.9).

Surgical abortion: Less is known about complications following surgical abortion, in part because fewer women present for follow-up. In a cohort study of early first-trimester abortions, of 16,925 women undergoing the procedure, only women who experienced persistent symptoms or had postoperative concerns (18%) returned. Of these women, 27 had ongoing pregnancy and 76 women (0.4%) underwent aspiration for persistent pain and/or bleeding.

Either medication or surgical abortion: In a study of 54,911 abortions occurring in 2009 to 2010 among 50,273 fee-for-service Medi-Cal beneficiaries, 478 (0.87% or 1 in 115) resulted in an emergency department visit for an abortion-related complication within 6 weeks. Only 15 (0.03%) involved ambulance transfers to EDs on the day of the abortion. The total abortion-related complication rate including all sources of care was 5.2% (n = 588) for medication abortion, 1.3% (n = 438) for first-trimester aspiration abortion, and 1.5% (n = 130) for second-trimester or later procedures. The major complication rate was 0.31% for medication abortion, 0.16% for first-trimester aspiration abortion, and 0.41% for second-trimester or later procedures.

Among women with private health insurance who had an induced first-trimester medication or surgical abortion or second-trimester abortion, performance of the 44,651 (89%) abortions in an office-based setting was comparable to performance of the 5660 abortions in an ambulatory surgery center with respect to abortion-related major morbidities or adverse events (0.26% vs. 0.33%).

National case-fatality rate for legal induced abortion for 2013 to 2018 was 0.41 deaths per 100,000. This case-fatality rate was lower than the rates for the previous two 5-year periods (0.6 and 0.65 deaths per 100,000).

The leading causes of death following abortion include anesthetic complications, infection, and hemorrhage. The risk of uterine rupture for second trimester abortion using misoprostol was 0.04% (95% CI, 0.01%-0.20%) in women without prior cesarean delivery and 0.28% (95% CI, 0.08%-1.00%) in women with prior cesarean delivery.

Induced abortion in the U.S. is associated with lower maternal mortality than childbirth (0.41 per 100,000 abortions vs. 17.4 per 100,000 live births; 660 maternal deaths in 2018) and lower morbidity (eg, relative risks for live births of 1.3 for mental health conditions, 4.4 for postpartum hemorrhage, 5.2 for obstetric infections).(data from Commonwealth Fund 2020)
Induced abortion does not result in a demonstrable increase in psychiatric disturbances, infertility, or cancer. B

In a review of 7 cohort studies with over 12,000 women, the incidence of miscarriage and postpartum hemorrhage was lower in the pregnancy following a medication abortion compared with a surgical abortion. No differences in subsequent pregnancy outcomes, however, were found in a large cohort study of 11,814 women in Denmark. B

Referral for further counseling should be available for the small minority of women who experience long-term postabortion distress. Risk factors for distress include ambivalence before the abortion, lack of a supportive partner, a psychiatric history, and membership of a cultural group that considers abortion wrong. C

ACOG (2014) recommends follow-up after completed surgical or medication abortion to diagnose and treat complications, including ongoing pregnancy. After surgical abortion, follow-up is recommended at 2 weeks.

ACOG (2020) notes that routine in-person follow-up is not necessary after uncomplicated medication abortion. Clinicians should offer patients the choice of self-assessment or clinical follow-up evaluation to assess medication abortion success. If medically indicated or preferred by the patient, ACOG recommends follow-up by medical history, clinical examination, serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) testing, or ultrasonography; the latter performed solely to determine presence or absence of a gestational sac.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found no differences in clinical outcomes (eg, missed ongoing pregnancy, unscheduled phone calls, surgical intervention) between self-assessment, remote assessment, or clinic follow-up for women undergoing medication abortion up to 10 weeks’ gestation. Data were of low quality, however.

In an RCT of 924 women who received abortions in four clinics in Austria, Finland, Norway, and Sweden, there was no difference in rates of complete abortion or need for additional surgery for women randomized to routine clinical follow-up or to self-assess outcome at home with a semiquantitative urine human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) test 1-3 weeks after abortion. There were 3 women in the self-assessment group who had undetected continuing pregnancies but more women in the clinic follow-up group who had infections (8 vs. 1).

ACOG 2020 recommends that all patients with a continuing pregnancy after using mifepristone and misoprostol should be provided with all pregnancy options and a thorough discussion of the risks and benefits of each.
Contraception should be discussed, and supplies or prescriptions provided if not previously done prior to the abortion (see above sections on treatment).

In an RCT of 748 patients undergoing first-trimester termination of pregnancy, those randomized to early IUD insertion, either during surgical abortion or 1 to 4 weeks following medication abortion, had fewer subsequent terminations in the 3 years following the procedure compared to women randomized to advice to contact their primary healthcare provider for follow-up and IUD insertion (10.7% vs. 16.9%, respectively). While the number of terminations was reduced during years 0-3 (22.2 vs. 46.5/1000), this was no longer significant at years 4-5 (33.3 vs. 26.8/1000).
Consider counseling perimenopausal women to continue contraceptive methods until age 55 years.

State laws restricting abortion services for minors can create barriers to care resulting in later-term abortions. See the Guttmacher Institute Web site for monthly updated abortion laws (www.agi-usa.org).
